source_artifacts.locator: approval card (as shown to the clerk)

capabilities.target: vendor master record, including bank details
payment to vendor bank account on file

inputs.source: Supplier invoices uploaded to the supplier portal

instructions.note: The agent is instructed to update vendor bank details whenever 'the invoice shows new bank details', with no requirement to validate the new account through any channel independent of the invoice itself. Invoice content is attacker-controllable (classic vendor-bank-change invoice fraud / BEC pattern).

The only stated safeguard for bank changes and payments is a model-generated 'one line summary' for clerk approval. The prompt does not require the summary, or the UI it drives, to show the bank account number, a diff of old vs new account, or PO match confidence. The approval card artifact confirms this: it shows only payee, amount, invoice number, and PO match, not the bank account change itself.

controls.name: Clerk approval card before payment or bank change
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced outside the model (orchestration blocks the action pending clerk approval), but the approver sees only the model's one-line summary, not the bank account number or change history (runtime notes). A more persuasive model writes a more convincing, selectively incomplete summary (ASI09). Effectiveness also degrades with approval volume (~150 cards/day), consistent with consent-fatigue (SAFE-T1403).

controls.name: Out-of-band verification of vendor bank detail changes
controls.decay_rationale: If implemented as a destination confirmation bound to a trusted record (e.g., a callback to the phone number already on file, not one supplied in the invoice), it blocks the change regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Raw-action approval review for bank and payment changes
controls.decay_rationale: A raw_action review mode would show the approver the actual bank account number, the diff from the prior value, and the payment destination from the system of record, rather than relying on the model's description.

controls.name: Least-privilege ERP credential scoping
controls.decay_rationale: Runtime notes state the ERP credential 'can update any vendor and schedule any payment'. Scoping this credential (e.g., per-vendor limits, payment amount caps) would not decay with model capability.

findings.title: TC9/TC4: Fraudulent invoice drives vendor bank-detail change behind a summary-only approval gate

attack_path.note: Attacker-controlled invoice uploaded to the supplier portal claims 'new bank details' for an existing vendor.
Agent reads the vendor master to match invoice to vendor and PO.
Agent updates the vendor's bank account on file based solely on the invoice's claim, gated only by a one-line approval summary that does not show the account number or change history.

forecast.watch_signal: Runtime notes already state the model is upgraded with the platform with no separate review. Watch the clerk's approval accept-rate on bank-change cards and whether the card ever surfaces the raw account number or change diff; also watch whether approval volume per clerk per day keeps rising.

evidence.observation: "If the invoice shows new bank details, update the vendor record" - the agent treats untrusted invoice content as authoritative for a sensitive financial record change.

evidence.locator: approval card (as shown to the clerk)
evidence.observation: The card shows only payee, amount, invoice id, and PO match - it does not disclose that a bank account is being changed, let alone the old vs new account number.
"Bank account numbers and the change history are not shown" and the clerk approves roughly 150 cards per day, consistent with approval fatigue (SAFE-T1403).

recommendations.action: Require out-of-band verification of any vendor bank detail change (e.g., a callback to the phone number already on file, never one supplied in the invoice) before the change is applied, independent of model judgment.
Change the approval card to raw_action review mode: show the current and proposed bank account number and the change history, not just a model-written summary.
Scope the ERP credential so the agent cannot update arbitrary vendor records without a secondary control path.

findings.title: TC9: Payment scheduled to a fraudulently-updated vendor bank account behind a summary-only approval gate

attack_path.note: Attacker-controlled invoice claims new bank details and a due amount.
Agent matches invoice to vendor and PO.
Agent updates the vendor's bank account on file, approved via a summary card that does not mention the bank change.
Agent schedules payment to the vendor's (now attacker-controlled) bank account, approved via a card that shows only payee name, amount, invoice id, and PO match.

forecast.watch_signal: Same signal as the bank-detail finding: unreviewed model upgrades and high-volume, summary-only approvals. Additionally watch for any payment approved shortly after a bank-detail change on the same vendor, which the current card design would not flag.

evidence.observation: "Schedule payment on the due date. Before any payment or bank change, request approval with a one line summary" - the same weak gate covers both the bank change and the payment, with no linkage shown between a recent bank change and the payment being approved.

evidence.locator: approval card (as shown to the clerk)
evidence.observation: "Pay Northwind Supplies $4,200.00 for INV-1187 (matches PO-5521)" - a plausible-looking card gives no indication that the destination account was changed moments earlier based on unverified invoice content.
"The ERP credential can update any vendor and schedule any payment" - the agent's credential scope is broad enough to both corrupt the vendor record and move funds against it.

recommendations.action: Block or specially flag any payment to a vendor whose bank details changed within N days, pending the out-of-band verification recommended for the bank-change finding.
Add anomaly detection on the sequence 'bank detail change followed by payment to the same vendor' and alert a second reviewer.
Cap or load-balance daily approvals per clerk, and require a second approver specifically for payments following a recent bank-detail change, to counter approval fatigue.

rating.rationale: Both findings start at critical because an untrusted input (a supplier invoice, which anyone who can reach the supplier portal can author) reaches two irreversible, high-value sinks: an ERP vendor bank-detail write and a payment spend, both using a broad, non-least-privilege credential. The only control in place, a human approval gate, is structural and present today, which credits a floor-limited two-tier reduction to 'moderate' per the rubric -- but it is a model_summary gate: the clerk sees only a one-line, model-written description (confirmed by the approval card artifact and the runtime notes, which state bank account numbers and change history are not shown). That makes the gate partially_dependent rather than independent. The runtime notes also state the model is upgraded with the platform with no separate review, which is exactly the model_upgrade trigger that defeats a model_summary gate per control_decay.md. Removing that gate's credit returns both findings to their inherent critical level, which drives the forecast. The single highest-leverage fix is converting the approval gate to raw_action review (showing the actual bank account and its change history) and adding an out-of-band verification step that is independent of the invoice content and of model behavior.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration shown in prompt.md, the approval card artifact, and the runtime notes. It does not reflect observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.

No tool manifest, MCP configuration, or IaC was provided. The ERP capabilities, their credential scope, and their reversibility are inferred from the stable id table and the runtime notes' statement that the credential 'can update any vendor and schedule any payment'; confidence on exact technical boundaries (e.g., whether any amount caps exist) is medium.

No information was given about any PO-matching fraud checks, vendor master audit trail, or system-of-record controls that might exist outside the described approval card. If such controls exist but were not described in the artifacts, actual residual risk could be lower than assessed here.
Attack paths were limited to the capabilities and inputs named in the stable id table; no additional egress channels (for example, notification emails) were described and none are assumed.
